Partial Differential Equations

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • classify a second-order linear PDE from its principal part;

  • distinguish the propagation behavior of elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic, and dispersive equations;

  • solve rectangular-domain problems by separation of variables; and

  • use Fourier or Laplace transforms to reduce a linear PDE to ODEs.

General Form of a Second-Order PDE¶

  • A general second-order linear PDE in two variables xxx and ttt can be written as:

A∂2u∂x2+B∂2u∂x∂t+C∂2u∂t2+lower-order terms=0,A \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + B \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial t} + C \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} + \text{lower-order terms} = 0,A∂x2∂2u​+B∂x∂t∂2u​+C∂t2∂2u​+lower-order terms=0,
(1)

where AAA, BBB, and CCC may depend on xxx and ttt. If they depend on the unknown uuu, the equation is no longer linear (though it may be quasilinear).

  • PDEs can be classified as elliptic, hyperbolic, or parabolic based on the discriminant of their highest-order terms:

Δ=B2−4AC.\Delta = B^2 - 4AC.Δ=B2−4AC.
(2)

  • The PDE is classified as:

    • Elliptic: Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 (B2−4AC<0B^2 - 4AC < 0B2−4AC<0),

    • Hyperbolic: Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0 (B2−4AC>0B^2 - 4AC > 0B2−4AC>0),

    • Parabolic: Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 (B2−4AC=0B^2 - 4AC = 0B2−4AC=0).

  • This classification influences the behavior of solutions and the types of physical phenomena the PDE describes.

Elliptic PDEs¶

Definition: Elliptic PDEs are characterized by Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0. They describe static or equilibrium states without inherent time evolution.

Canonical Example: Laplace’s equation:

∇2u=0or∂2u∂x2+∂2u∂y2=0.\nabla^2 u = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0.∇2u=0or∂x2∂2u​+∂y2∂2u​=0.
(3)

Properties:

  • Nature of Solutions: Smooth and globally influenced; the solution at any point depends on the boundary conditions over the entire domain.

  • Physical Interpretation: Models static or steady-state phenomena such as:

    • Electrostatics (∇2ϕ=0\nabla^2 \phi = 0∇2ϕ=0),

    • Heat conduction in equilibrium,

    • velocity potentials for incompressible, irrotational flow.

  • Boundary Conditions: Elliptic PDEs require boundary conditions (e.g., Dirichlet or Neumann conditions).

Hyperbolic PDEs¶

Definition: Hyperbolic PDEs are characterized by Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0. They describe systems with wave-like or propagative behavior.

Canonical Example: The wave equation:

∂2u∂t2−c2∂2u∂x2=0.\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} - c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 0.∂t2∂2u​−c2∂x2∂2u​=0.
(4)

Properties:

  • Nature of Solutions: Governed by causality; the solution at a given point depends only on the initial and boundary data within its causal domain (e.g., the light cone in relativistic systems).

  • Physical Interpretation: Models dynamic phenomena involving wave propagation, such as:

    • Vibrations of a string or membrane,

    • Electromagnetic waves,

    • Sound waves in a medium.

  • Initial and Boundary Conditions: A second-order wave equation requires initial displacement and velocity. Boundary conditions are also required on bounded spatial domains.

Parabolic PDEs¶

A PDE is classified as parabolic if the coefficients A,B, and C satisfy the condition B2=4ACB^2=4ACB2=4AC

Canonical Example: The diffusion equation (or heat equation):

κ∂2u∂x2=∂u∂t\kappa \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} =\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}κ∂x2∂2u​=∂t∂u​
(5)

Properties:

  • Nature of Solutions:

    • Solutions become infinitely smooth instantly, even if the initial data is rough. This comes from the diffusion kernel (Gaussian), which convolves with the initial condition.

    • The maximum is controlled by initial and boundary values, which results in uniqueness of solutions.

    • Solutions depend continuously on initial data.

    • Unlike hyperbolic PDEs, parabolic PDEs have no finite wave speed.

  • Physical Interpretation: Propagation of heat, diffusion, chemical reactions

  • Initial and Boundary Conditions: Parabolic PDEs require one initial condition u(x,0)u(x,0)u(x,0) and boundary conditions (Dirichlet, Neumann).

Definition of Δ\DeltaΔ¶

The Laplacian (also called the Laplace operator) of a sufficiently smooth function u:Rn→Ru : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}u:Rn→R is defined as

Δu=∑i=1n∂2u∂xi2.\Delta u = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_i^2}.Δu=i=1∑n​∂xi2​∂2u​.
(6)

Special cases:

  • 1D: Δu=uxx\Delta u = u_{xx}Δu=uxx​

  • 2D: Δu=uxx+uyy\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}Δu=uxx​+uyy​

  • 3D: Δu=uxx+uyy+uzz\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} + u_{zz}Δu=uxx​+uyy​+uzz​

Wave Equation¶

utt=c2Δuu_{tt} = c^2 \Delta uutt​=c2Δu

Type: Hyperbolic

Models:

  • Vibrating strings and membranes

  • Sound waves

  • Electromagnetic waves (in simplified form)

Properties:

  • Finite propagation speed

  • Energy is conserved for appropriate homogeneous boundary conditions

  • Well-posed with initial position and velocity

Diffusion (Heat) Equation¶

ut=κ Δuu_t = \kappa\, \Delta uut​=κΔu
(12)

Type: Parabolic

Models:

  • Heat conduction

  • Diffusion of particles or chemicals

  • Brownian motion via probability density evolution

Properties:

  • Infinite propagation speed (instant smoothing)

  • Maximum principle applies

  • Solutions become smoother for t>0t>0t>0

Fundamental Solution (Heat Kernel):

K(x,t)=14πκtexp⁡ ⁣(−x24κt),t>0,K(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi \kappa t}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{4\kappa t}\right), \qquad t>0,K(x,t)=4πκt​1​exp(−4κtx2​),t>0,
(13)

which is the solution for a unit point-source initial condition on the real line. General initial data are convolved with KKK.

Laplace Equation¶

Δu=0\Delta u = 0Δu=0
(14)

Models:

  • Electrostatics (potential fields)

  • Steady heat flow

  • Incompressible fluid potential flow

Properties:

  • No time evolution

Poisson Equation¶

Δu=f(x)\Delta u = f(x)Δu=f(x)
(16)

Type: Elliptic

Models:

  • Potentials generated by sources

  • Electrostatics with charge density

  • Gravitational potential in Newtonian gravity

Properties:

  • Requires boundary conditions

  • Elliptic regularity often makes solutions smoother than the source, subject to domain and boundary regularity

  • Green’s function representation

Function fff is called the source density

for a free-space solution decaying at infinity. The minus sign follows from Δ(1/r)=−4πδ(r)\Delta(1/r)=-4\pi\delta(\mathbf r)Δ(1/r)=−4πδ(r).

Poisson’s Equation in Electrostatics¶

Electric potential ϕ(r)\phi(\mathbf{r})ϕ(r) satisfies:

Δϕ(r)=− ρ(r)ε0\Delta \phi(\mathbf{r}) = -\,\frac{\rho(\mathbf{r})}{\varepsilon_0}Δϕ(r)=−ε0​ρ(r)​
(18)

Where:

  • ρ(r)\rho(\mathbf{r})ρ(r) = charge density

  • ε0\varepsilon_0ε0​ = vacuum permittivity

Example: Point charge qqq at origin:

ρ(r)=q δ(r)\rho(\mathbf{r}) = q\, \delta(\mathbf{r})ρ(r)=qδ(r)
(19)

Solution: Coulomb potential

ϕ(r)=q4πε0 r,r=∥r∥\phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0\, r}, \quad r = \|\mathbf{r}\|ϕ(r)=4πε0​rq​,r=∥r∥
(20)

Poisson’s Equation in Newtonian Gravity¶

Gravitational potential Φ(r)\Phi(\mathbf{r})Φ(r) satisfies:

ΔΦ(r)=4πG ρ(r)\Delta \Phi(\mathbf{r}) = 4\pi G\, \rho(\mathbf{r})ΔΦ(r)=4πGρ(r)
(21)

Where:

  • ρ(r)\rho(\mathbf{r})ρ(r) = mass density

  • GGG = gravitational constant

Example: Point mass MMM at origin:

ρ(r)=M δ(r)\rho(\mathbf{r}) = M\, \delta(\mathbf{r})ρ(r)=Mδ(r)
(22)

Solution: Newtonian potential

Φ(r)=−GMr,r=∥r∥\Phi(\mathbf{r}) = -\frac{GM}{r}, \quad r = \|\mathbf{r}\|Φ(r)=−rGM​,r=∥r∥
(23)

Separation of variables¶

Let’s consider the three-dimensional wave equation:

utt=c2Δu,Δu=uxx+uyy+uzzu_{tt} = c^2 \Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} + u_{zz}utt​=c2Δu,Δu=uxx​+uyy​+uzz​
(28)

Domain: Rectangular box 0<x<Lx0<x<L_x0<x<Lx​, 0<y<Ly0<y<L_y0<y<Ly​, 0<z<Lz0<z<L_z0<z<Lz​

Boundary conditions: Dirichlet

u(0,y,z,t)=u(Lx,y,z,t)=0,etc. for y,zu(0,y,z,t) = u(L_x,y,z,t) = 0, \quad \text{etc. for } y,zu(0,y,z,t)=u(Lx​,y,z,t)=0,etc. for y,z
(29)

Initial conditions:

u(x,y,z,0)=f(x,y,z),ut(x,y,z,0)=g(x,y,z)u(x,y,z,0) = f(x,y,z), \quad u_t(x,y,z,0) = g(x,y,z)u(x,y,z,0)=f(x,y,z),ut​(x,y,z,0)=g(x,y,z)
(30)

Step 1: Assume Separable Solution¶

Assume a solution of the form:

u(x,y,z,t)=X(x) Y(y) Z(z) T(t)u(x,y,z,t) = X(x)\, Y(y)\, Z(z)\, T(t)u(x,y,z,t)=X(x)Y(y)Z(z)T(t)
(31)

Substitute into the wave equation:

XYZ T′′=c2(X′′YZ+XY′′Z+XYZ′′)TX Y Z\, T'' = c^2 \left( X'' Y Z + X Y'' Z + X Y Z'' \right) TXYZT′′=c2(X′′YZ+XY′′Z+XYZ′′)T
(32)

Divide both sides by c2XYZTc^2XYZTc2XYZT:

T′′(t)c2T(t)=X′′(x)X(x)+Y′′(y)Y(y)+Z′′(z)Z(z)\frac{T''(t)}{c^2 T(t)} = \frac{X''(x)}{X(x)} + \frac{Y''(y)}{Y(y)} + \frac{Z''(z)}{Z(z)}c2T(t)T′′(t)​=X(x)X′′(x)​+Y(y)Y′′(y)​+Z(z)Z′′(z)​
(33)

Each side depends on different variables   ⟹  \implies⟹ must equal a constant:

X′′X+Y′′Y+Z′′Z=−λ2,T′′+c2λ2T=0\frac{X''}{X} + \frac{Y''}{Y} + \frac{Z''}{Z} = -\lambda^2, \quad T'' + c^2 \lambda^2 T = 0XX′′​+YY′′​+ZZ′′​=−λ2,T′′+c2λ2T=0
(34)

Step 2: Solve Spatial Equations¶

Split spatial part into three 1D problems:

X′′+kx2X=0,Y′′+ky2Y=0,Z′′+kz2Z=0X'' + k_x^2 X = 0, \quad Y'' + k_y^2 Y = 0, \quad Z'' + k_z^2 Z = 0X′′+kx2​X=0,Y′′+ky2​Y=0,Z′′+kz2​Z=0
(35)

Boundary conditions:

X(0)=X(Lx)=0  ⟹  Xn(x)=sin⁡(nπxLx),  n=1,2,...X(0)=X(L_x)=0 \implies X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L_x}\right),\; n=1,2,...X(0)=X(Lx​)=0⟹Xn​(x)=sin(Lx​nπx​),n=1,2,...
(36)

Similarly:

Ym(y)=sin⁡(mπyLy),Zp(z)=sin⁡(pπzLz)Y_m(y) = \sin\left(\frac{m \pi y}{L_y}\right),\quad Z_p(z) = \sin\left(\frac{p \pi z}{L_z}\right)Ym​(y)=sin(Ly​mπy​),Zp​(z)=sin(Lz​pπz​)
(37)

Eigenvalues:

kx=nπLx,ky=mπLy,kz=pπLzk_x = \frac{n\pi}{L_x},\quad k_y = \frac{m\pi}{L_y},\quad k_z = \frac{p\pi}{L_z}kx​=Lx​nπ​,ky​=Ly​mπ​,kz​=Lz​pπ​
(38)
λ2=kx2+ky2+kz2\lambda^2 = k_x^2 + k_y^2 + k_z^2λ2=kx2​+ky2​+kz2​
(39)

Step 3: Solve Temporal Equation¶

Temporal equation:

T′′+c2λ2T=0T'' + c^2 \lambda^2 T = 0T′′+c2λ2T=0
(40)

General solution:

Tnmp(t)=Anmpcos⁡(cλt)+Bnmpsin⁡(cλt)T_{nmp}(t) = A_{nmp} \cos(c \lambda t) + B_{nmp} \sin(c \lambda t)Tnmp​(t)=Anmp​cos(cλt)+Bnmp​sin(cλt)
(41)

λ2=kx2+ky2+kz2\lambda^2 = k_x^2 + k_y^2 + k_z^2λ2=kx2​+ky2​+kz2​

Step 4: Construct Full Solution¶

Combine spatial and temporal parts:

u(x,y,z,t)=∑n,m,p=1∞sin⁡(nπxLx)sin⁡(mπyLy)sin⁡(pπzLz)u(x,y,z,t) = \sum_{n,m,p=1}^{\infty} \sin\Big(\frac{n\pi x}{L_x}\Big) \sin\Big(\frac{m\pi y}{L_y}\Big) \sin\Big(\frac{p\pi z}{L_z}\Big)u(x,y,z,t)=n,m,p=1∑∞​sin(Lx​nπx​)sin(Ly​mπy​)sin(Lz​pπz​)
(42)
×[Anmpcos⁡(cλnmpt)+Bnmpsin⁡(cλnmpt)]\times\Big[ A_{nmp} \cos(c \lambda_{nmp} t) + B_{nmp} \sin(c \lambda_{nmp} t) \Big]×[Anmp​cos(cλnmp​t)+Bnmp​sin(cλnmp​t)]
(43)
λnmp=(nπLx)2+(mπLy)2+(pπLz)2\lambda_{nmp} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{n\pi}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{m\pi}{L_y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{p\pi}{L_z}\right)^2}λnmp​=(Lx​nπ​)2+(Ly​mπ​)2+(Lz​pπ​)2​
(44)

Constants Anmp,BnmpA_{nmp}, B_{nmp}Anmp​,Bnmp​ are determined from initial conditions via Fourier series.

Summary¶

  • Assumed separable solution: u(x,y,z,t)=XYZTu(x,y,z,t) = X Y Z Tu(x,y,z,t)=XYZT

  • Reduced PDE to ODEs in xxx, yyy, zzz, ttt

  • Applied boundary conditions to find spatial eigenfunctions

  • Solved temporal ODE to get oscillatory time dependence

  • Superposed all modes using Fourier series to satisfy initial conditions

Key Takeaway: Separation of variables converts a multi-dimensional PDE into simpler 1D ODEs, which can be solved systematically.

The Superposition Principle¶

The Superposition Principle¶

The Superposition Principle enables the construction of the overall solution:

  • Separation of Variables generates independent ODEs coupled by [separation constants]{.alert} λ\lambdaλ.

  • This yields a family of particular solutions,uλi(x,y)u_{\lambda_i} (x,y)uλi​​(x,y).

  • Multiple Solutions: If individual solutions u1,u2,…u_1, u_2, \dotsu1​,u2​,… satisfy the linear PDE, then any weighted sum of these solutions also satisfies the PDE.

  • General Solution: The general solution u(x,y)u(x,y)u(x,y) is formed by the linear superposition (weighted sum) of all allowed solutions:

u(x,y)=∑iaiXλi(x)Yλi(y)u(x, y) = \sum_i a_i X_{\lambda_i}(x)Y_{\lambda_i}(y)u(x,y)=i∑​ai​Xλi​​(x)Yλi​​(y)
(45)

  • Role of Boundary Conditions: The linear superposition is necessary because it creates a flexible general solution that can be matched to the specific boundary conditions imposed by the physical problem.

Example: Laplace’s Equation (Steady-State Temperature)¶

Consider a semi-infinite rectangular plate whose edges are kept at fixed temperature:

∂2u∂x2+∂2u∂y2=0\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 \quad∂x2∂2u​+∂y2∂2u​=0
(46)

Homogeneous Boundary Conditions (BCs):

  • u(x,0)=0u(x,0)=0u(x,0)=0 (Bottom edge)

  • u(x,b)=0u(x,b)=0u(x,b)=0 (Top edge)

  • u(∞,y)=0u(\infty,y)=0u(∞,y)=0 (Far edge)

Example: Laplace’s Equation (Steady-State Temperature) (continued)¶

∂2u∂x2+∂2u∂y2=0\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0 \quad∂x2∂2u​+∂y2∂2u​=0
(47)

Separated Solution and Eigenvalues:

  • Applying the BCs leads to solutions of the form u(x,y)∝exp⁡(−λx)sin⁡(λy)u(x,y)\propto \exp(-\lambda x)\sin(\lambda y)u(x,y)∝exp(−λx)sin(λy).

  • The constraints imposed by the geometry and BCs quantize the separation constant λ\lambdaλ to discrete values:

λn=nπb,n=1,2,3,…\lambda_n = \frac{n\pi}{b}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dotsλn​=bnπ​,n=1,2,3,…
(48)

Constructing the Fourier Series Solution¶

Since uuu must satisfy the linear PDE for all allowed values of λn\lambda_nλn​, the general solution is the superposition of these elemental solutions: Superposed Solution:

u(x,y)=∑n=1∞Bnexp⁡(−nπxb)sin⁡(nπyb)u(x, y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \exp\left(-\frac{n\pi x}{b}\right) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi y}{b}\right)u(x,y)=n=1∑∞​Bn​exp(−bnπx​)sin(bnπy​)
(49)

Matching the Inhomogeneous BC: The arbitrary coefficients BnB_nBn​ are now determined by the final boundary condition, u(0,y)=f(y)u(0,y)=f(y)u(0,y)=f(y):

f(y)=∑n=1∞Bnsin⁡(nπyb)f(y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \sin\left(\frac{n\pi y}{b}\right)f(y)=n=1∑∞​Bn​sin(bnπy​)
(50)

  • This expression is a [Fourier sine series]{.alert}.

  • The coefficients BnB_nBn​ are found using the orthogonality of the sine functions (a fundamental principle of [eigenfunction expansion]{.alert}).

Example: Solving heat equation using Fourier transform¶

  • The Heat (Diffusion) Equation in the Spatial Domain:

∂u∂t=α2∂2u∂x2orut=α2uxx\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \quad \text{or} \quad u_t = \alpha^2 u_{xx}∂t∂u​=α2∂x2∂2u​orut​=α2uxx​
(51)

where u(t,x)u(t,x)u(t,x) is the temperature distribution and α2\alpha^2α2 is the thermal diffusivity.

  • Apply the Fourier transform in space:

F(u(t,x))=u^(t,ω)\mathcal{F}(u(t, x)) = \hat{u}(t,\omega)F(u(t,x))=u^(t,ω)
(52)

.

  • Utilize the property of the Fourier transform derivatives :

F(uxx)=(iω)2u^=−ω2u^\mathcal{F}(u_{xx}) = (\text{i}\omega)^2 \hat{u} = -\omega^2 \hat{u}F(uxx​)=(iω)2u^=−ω2u^
(53)

  • Applying this transformation, the original PDE is converted into an ODE for each fixed frequency ω\omegaω:

u^t=−α2ω2u^\hat{u}_t = -\alpha^2 \omega^2 \hat{u}u^t​=−α2ω2u^
(54)

Example: Solving heat equation using Fourier transform (continued)¶

  • The resulting ODE in the frequency domain has a straightforward exponential solution

u^(t,ω)=e−α2ω2tu^(0,ω)\hat{u}(t, \omega) = e^{-\alpha^2\omega^2 t} \hat{u}(0, \omega)u^(t,ω)=e−α2ω2tu^(0,ω)
(55)

where u^(0,ω)\hat{u}(0, \omega)u^(0,ω) is the Fourier transform of the initial temperature distribution u(0,x)u(0, x)u(0,x).

This solution shows that higher frequencies (larger ω\omegaω) decay more rapidly.

  • To find the solution u(t,x)u(t, x)u(t,x) in the original coordinates, the inverse Fourier transform is applied to u^(t,ω)\hat{u}(t, \omega)u^(t,ω):

u(t,x)=F−1(u^(t,ω))u(t, x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{u}(t, \omega))u(t,x)=F−1(u^(t,ω))
(56)

Using the convolution theorem, the solution is the convolution of the initial condition u(0,x)u(0, x)u(0,x) with the inverse transform of the Gaussian term, which is also a Gaussian:

u(t,x)=F−1(e−α2ω2t)∗u(0,x)=12απte−x24α2t∗u(0,x)u(t, x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(e^{-\alpha^2\omega^2 t}\right) \ast u(0, x) = \frac{1}{2\alpha \sqrt{\pi t}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{4 \alpha^2 t}} \ast u(0, x)u(t,x)=F−1(e−α2ω2t)∗u(0,x)=2απt​1​e−4α2tx2​∗u(0,x)
(57)

Laplace Transform: Definition¶

The Laplace transform of a function f(t)f(t)f(t) is defined as:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t) dt\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \, dtL{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt
(58)

Properties:

  • Linearity: L{af+bg}=aF+bG\mathcal{L}\{a f + b g\} = a F + b GL{af+bg}=aF+bG

  • Derivative in time: L{f′(t)}=sF(s)−f(0)\mathcal{L}\{f'(t)\} = s F(s) - f(0)L{f′(t)}=sF(s)−f(0)

  • Reduces differential equations in ttt to algebraic equations in sss

Step 1: PDE Example¶

Consider the 1D heat equation:

ut=α2uxx,0<x<L,  t>0u_t = \alpha^2 u_{xx}, \qquad 0 < x < L, \; t>0ut​=α2uxx​,0<x<L,t>0
(59)

Initial condition: u(x,0)=f(x)u(x,0) = f(x)u(x,0)=f(x)

Boundary conditions: u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0

Step 2: Apply Laplace Transform in Time¶

Take Laplace transform w.r.t ttt:

L{ut}=suˉ(x,s)−u(x,0)\mathcal{L}\{u_t\} = s \bar{u}(x,s) - u(x,0)L{ut​}=suˉ(x,s)−u(x,0)
(60)

⇒\Rightarrow⇒ PDE becomes an ODE in xxx:

suˉ(x,s)−f(x)=α2uˉxx(x,s)s \bar{u}(x,s) - f(x) = \alpha^2 \bar{u}_{xx}(x,s)suˉ(x,s)−f(x)=α2uˉxx​(x,s)
(61)
uˉxx−sα2uˉ=−f(x)α2\bar{u}_{xx} - \frac{s}{\alpha^2} \bar{u} = - \frac{f(x)}{\alpha^2}uˉxx​−α2s​uˉ=−α2f(x)​
(62)

Boundary conditions in Laplace domain: uˉ(0,s)=uˉ(L,s)=0\bar{u}(0,s) = \bar{u}(L,s) = 0uˉ(0,s)=uˉ(L,s)=0

Step 3: Solve the Spatial ODE¶

The transformed equation is a linear second-order ODE:

uˉxx−sα2uˉ=−f(x)α2\bar{u}_{xx} - \frac{s}{\alpha^2} \bar{u} = - \frac{f(x)}{\alpha^2}uˉxx​−α2s​uˉ=−α2f(x)​
(63)

Homogeneous solution:

uˉh(x,s)=Asinh⁡(sα2 x)+Bsinh⁡(sα2(L−x))\bar{u}_h(x,s) = A \sinh\left(\sqrt{\frac{s}{\alpha^2}}\, x \right) + B \sinh\left(\sqrt{\frac{s}{\alpha^2}} (L-x)\right)uˉh​(x,s)=Asinh(α2s​​x)+Bsinh(α2s​​(L−x))
(64)

Particular solution: depends on f(x)f(x)f(x)

Apply boundary conditions to determine constants A,BA,BA,B

Obtaining the Particular Solution Using Eigenfunction Expansion¶

Inhomogeneous ODE in Laplace domain:

uˉxx−sα2uˉ=−f(x)α2,uˉ(0,s)=uˉ(L,s)=0\bar{u}_{xx} - \frac{s}{\alpha^2} \bar{u} = -\frac{f(x)}{\alpha^2}, \quad \bar{u}(0,s) = \bar{u}(L,s) = 0uˉxx​−α2s​uˉ=−α2f(x)​,uˉ(0,s)=uˉ(L,s)=0
(65)

1. Expand the initial condition in eigenfunctions (sine series):

f(x)=∑n=1∞Fnsin⁡(nπxL),Fn=2L∫0Lf(x)sin⁡(nπxL)dxf(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right), \quad F_n = \frac{2}{L} \int_0^L f(x) \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) dxf(x)=n=1∑∞​Fn​sin(Lnπx​),Fn​=L2​∫0L​f(x)sin(Lnπx​)dx
(66)

2. Look for a particular solution in the same basis:

uˉp(x,s)=∑n=1∞Uˉn(s)sin⁡(nπxL)\bar{u}_p(x,s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bar{U}_n(s) \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right)uˉp​(x,s)=n=1∑∞​Uˉn​(s)sin(Lnπx​)
(67)

3. Substitute into the ODE and solve algebraically for each mode:

Uˉn(s)=Fns+α2(nπ/L)2\bar{U}_n(s) = \frac{F_n}{s + \alpha^2 (n \pi / L)^2}Uˉn​(s)=s+α2(nπ/L)2Fn​​
(68)

4. Inverse Laplace transform: u(x,t)=∑n=1∞Fnsin⁡(nπxL)e−α2(nπ/L)2tu(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) e^{-\alpha^2 (n \pi / L)^2 t}u(x,t)=∑n=1∞​Fn​sin(Lnπx​)e−α2(nπ/L)2t

Step 4: Inverse Laplace Transform¶

Once uˉ(x,s)\bar{u}(x,s)uˉ(x,s) is determined, the solution in time is obtained by inverse Laplace transform:

u(x,t)=L−1{uˉ(x,s)}=12πi∫γ−i∞γ+i∞estuˉ(x,s) dsu(x,t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{\bar{u}(x,s)\} = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\gamma - i\infty}^{\gamma + i\infty} e^{st} \bar{u}(x,s)\, dsu(x,t)=L−1{uˉ(x,s)}=2πi1​∫γ−i∞γ+i∞​estuˉ(x,s)ds
(69)

Example for simple initial condition: f(x)=sin⁡(nπxL)f(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)f(x)=sin(Lnπx​)

uˉ(x,s)=sin⁡(nπxL)s+α2(nπ/L)2⇒u(x,t)=sin⁡(nπxL)e−α2(nπ/L)2t\bar{u}(x,s) = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right)}{s + \alpha^2 (n\pi/L)^2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad u(x,t) = \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) e^{-\alpha^2 (n\pi/L)^2 t}uˉ(x,s)=s+α2(nπ/L)2sin(Lnπx​)​⇒u(x,t)=sin(Lnπx​)e−α2(nπ/L)2t
(70)

Summary of the Method¶

  1. Take Laplace transform in time (or other variable) to reduce PDE to ODE.

  2. Solve the resulting ODE in space (or other variable) with boundary conditions.

  3. Apply the inverse Laplace transform to return to the original variable.

  4. Superpose solutions if initial/boundary conditions are decomposed in eigenfunctions.

Key Advantage: Converts time derivatives into algebraic terms, simplifying the solution of linear PDEs.

Homework for this lecture¶

Problem from Jonathan’s original homework¶

Consider the one-dimensional diffusion equation

∂u∂t=D∂2u∂x2,0<x<L,\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=D\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}, \qquad 0<x<L,∂t∂u​=D∂x2∂2u​,0<x<L,
(71)

with homogeneous boundary conditions u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0.

  1. Substitute u(x,t)=X(x)T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t) and derive the two ordinary differential equations, including a consistent choice of separation constant.

  2. Find the allowed spatial eigenfunctions and their corresponding temporal factors.

  3. Write the series solution for an arbitrary initial profile u(x,0)=f(x)u(x,0)=f(x)u(x,0)=f(x) and give the integral formula for its expansion coefficients.

Existing final-project option¶

Objective {#objective .unnumbered}¶

In this project you will derive, analyze, and numerically solve differential equations that arise when Michaelis--Menten reaction kinetics are coupled to transport processes. You will work with both first--order nonlinear ODEs and a second--order nonlinear boundary--value problem.

Physical Background {#physical-background .unnumbered}¶

Consider the enzymatic reaction

E+S⇌k1k−1ES  →kcat  E+P,E + S \underset{k_{-1}}{\stackrel{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} ES \;\xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}\; E + P,E+Sk−1​⇌k1​​​ESkcat​​E+P,
(72)

which under the quasi--steady--state approximation leads to the Michaelis--Menten rate law

v(S)=Vmax⁡ SKM+S,Vmax⁡=kcat[E]0,KM=k−1+kcatk1.v(S) = \frac{V_{\max}\, S}{K_M + S}, \qquad V_{\max} = k_{\mathrm{cat}} [E]_0, \qquad K_M = \frac{k_{-1} + k_{\mathrm{cat}}}{k_1}.v(S)=KM​+SVmax​S​,Vmax​=kcat​[E]0​,KM​=k1​k−1​+kcat​​.
(73)

You will examine three scenarios:

  1. A well--mixed batch reactor.

  2. A plug--flow reactor with spatial variation.

  3. A reaction--diffusion system in a one--dimensional medium.

Tasks {#tasks .unnumbered}¶

1. Batch Reactor (Well-Mixed System)¶

Starting from the Michaelis--Menten rate law, derive an ODE for the time evolution of the substrate concentration S(t)S(t)S(t) in a well-mixed batch reactor:

dSdt=−Vmax⁡ SKM+S.\frac{dS}{dt} = - \frac{V_{\max}\, S}{K_M + S}.dtdS​=−KM​+SVmax​S​.
(74)

Hints:

  • Write a mass balance using “Rate of accumulation = Rate of reaction”.

  • The resulting equation is separable.

  • Express the solution implicitly (explicit solution in closed form is not required).

2. Plug-Flow Reactor (Steady State, No Diffusion)¶

Consider steady flow with velocity vvv through a tubular reactor of length LLL. Let S(x)S(x)S(x) be the substrate concentration along the tube. Show that the governing ODE becomes

v dSdx=−Vmax⁡ SKM+S.v\,\frac{dS}{dx} = -\frac{V_{\max}\, S}{K_M + S}.vdxdS​=−KM​+SVmax​S​.
(75)

Hints:

  • Use a steady-state mass balance on a differential slice of the reactor.

  • The resulting ODE is first-order and nonlinear.

  • Specify an inlet boundary condition S(0)=S0S(0)=S_0S(0)=S0​.

3. Reaction--Diffusion System (Steady State)¶

Now assume the substrate diffuses in a one-dimensional medium (e.g., an enzyme-filled gel or catalyst pellet). Let DDD be the diffusion coefficient. At steady state, derive the equation

Dd2Sdx2=Vmax⁡ SKM+S.D \frac{d^2 S}{dx^2} = \frac{V_{\max}\, S}{K_M + S}.Ddx2d2S​=KM​+SVmax​S​.
(76)

This is a nonlinear second-order boundary-value problem.

Hints:

  • Start from the steady-state diffusion--reaction equation

D d2Sdx2−R(S)=0,R(S)=Vmax⁡SKM+S.D\,\frac{d^2 S}{dx^2} - R(S) = 0, \qquad R(S) = \frac{V_{\max} S}{K_M + S}.Ddx2d2S​−R(S)=0,R(S)=KM​+SVmax​S​.
(77)

  • Choose physically meaningful boundary conditions (e.g., fixed concentration at the surface, zero-flux at a symmetry plane).

  • Consider nondimensionalizing the equation to identify important parameters.

4. Numerical Solution¶

Solve the reaction--diffusion boundary-value problem numerically.

5. Analysis and Discussion¶

Discuss:

  • How the profile S(x)S(x)S(x) depends on the ratio Vmax⁡/DV_{\max}/DVmax​/D.

  • Behavior in the limits S≪KMS \ll K_MS≪KM​ and S≫KMS \gg K_MS≫KM​.

  • How the nonlinear MM kinetics differ qualitatively from first-order kinetics.
